newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Latin America on heels of Asia in child sex abuse.
newsitem.headline: Latin America on heels of Asia in child sex abuse.

text.p: The level of sexual abuse of children in Latin America is approaching that in Asia, world experts gathered in Argentina said on Thursday.

"The distance between Asia and Latin America is not great," Agnes Fournier de Saint Maur of Interpol's general secretariat told Reuters. "What's happened is that Asia has taken measures to repress these criminal activities and they've automatically shifted to more fertile ground."
The three-day International Conference on Crimes Against Children, organised by Interpol, ended on Thursday in Buenos Aires with the participation of some 200 experts.

Earlier in the conference, Brazil's UNICEF delegate Arabela Rota said that in Latin America, pedophilia and prostitution were most widespread in Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and Cuba. She said poor, black women suffered the worst abuse.
Experts blame the situation on poverty and changing family structures, including rising numbers of single mothers.

"This forces the woman, who is responsible for the children, to spend long hours outside the home. The child is left virtually alone, seeks the streets and ends up as a prostitute," Uruguay's crime prevention director Graciela Lopez said.
Experts say sexual tourism has turned child abuse into a multimillion dollar industry.
In Brazil, the government is trying to clamp down and has placed banners in airports and hotels that read: "Exploitation of minors for sexual tourism: Beware, Brazil is watching you."

"Charter tours come from Germany, Italy, Switzerland and France," said Ana Quental, an organiser of the poster campaign. "We're talking about lower class tourists without much purchasing power. Apart from abusing our girls, they leave very little money in the country."
Northern Brazilian states, where the problem is most serious, are also trying to reform their police forces to make them more gentle and reliable when dealing with victims.

"You have to give the police a humane aspect, make them sensitive to abuse. Only that kind of police will be able to deal appropriately with defenceless people," Neto Gautier Amorin, a police lieutenant in Bahia, Brazil, told Reuters.
Fournier said one million children are forced into prostitution around the world and "pedophilia is rising ... We must make governments and society aware of it."
